note: Reference set. Every other seed file follows these patterns exactly. Authored by Claude — do not edit when adding new content, add a new file instead.

cards.meaning: saying what is needed in few words
examples: Her answer was concise — two lines, and I understood everything.
Keep the status update concise; nobody reads past the third line.
cards.say: Think of a message someone sent you that was far too long. Say one sentence about it using 'concise'.

cards.meaning: slow to act or speak because you are unsure
examples: He was hesitant to say what he really thought.
I'm hesitant to commit to that date until testing is done.
cards.say: Say a sentence about something you were unsure about committing to at work. Use 'hesitant'.

cards.meaning: sudden, and often rude because of it
examples: The call ended so abruptly that I thought the line had dropped.
Sorry if that came across as abrupt — I was between meetings.
cards.say: Describe a conversation that ended too suddenly. Use 'abrupt' or 'abruptly'.

cards.meaning: complete, with nothing left out
examples: She's thorough — she checks the things nobody asks about.
Give it one thorough pass before we send it to the client.
cards.say: Describe someone at work who checks everything properly. Use 'thorough'.

cards.meaning: boring because it is long and repetitive
examples: Filling that sheet by hand is tedious.
It's not difficult work, it's just tedious.
cards.say: Say one sentence about the most repetitive part of your week. Use 'tedious'.

cards.meaning: saying the truth directly, without softening it
examples: Can I be blunt? The deadline isn't realistic.
He's blunt, but you always know where you stand with him.
cards.say: Say something you'd normally soften — but say it bluntly. Start with 'Can I be blunt?'

cards.meaning: unwilling, and doing it anyway
examples: I was reluctant to take it on, but there was nobody else.
He gave a reluctant yes.
cards.say: Describe something you agreed to do but didn't want to. Use 'reluctant'.

cards.meaning: done on impulse, without planning it
examples: It was completely spontaneous — we just got in the car and left.
The best part of the evening was spontaneous.
cards.say: Describe the last unplanned thing you did. Use 'spontaneous'.

cards.meaning: return to a topic later, once there's more information
cards.scenario: Someone raises a good question in a meeting, but answering it properly would derail the agenda. Park it.
cards.example: Good question — let's circle back on that once we have the numbers.

cards.meaning: in agreement about what is happening and why
cards.scenario: Before a project starts, you want to confirm that everyone understood the plan the same way.
cards.example: Before we start building, I want to make sure we're all on the same page about scope.

cards.meaning: make a difference big enough to actually show up in the numbers
cards.scenario: You're arguing that a small tweak isn't worth the effort.
cards.example: Changing the button colour won't move the needle — the sign-up form is the problem.

cards.meaning: the time and attention someone has available
cards.scenario: You're being handed a third project and need to decline without sounding unwilling.
cards.example: I don't have the bandwidth for this before the 20th — can it wait, or should something else move?

cards.meaning: the easiest wins, worth doing first because they cost so little
cards.scenario: You're planning what to tackle first with limited time.
cards.example: Let's take the low-hanging fruit this sprint and leave the migration for next quarter.

cards.meaning: continue a discussion separately, outside the current meeting
cards.scenario: Two people are deep in a detail that only concerns them, and eight others are waiting.
cards.example: This is worth solving — can the two of you take it offline and report back?

cards.meaning: to catch your foot on something and lose your balance
cards.contrast: You TRIP on something — there's an obstacle. You SLIP on something — the surface is smooth. You STUMBLE after either one, while trying not to fall.
examples: I tripped on the last step and nearly went down.
He tripped over a cable someone had left across the floor.

cards.meaning: to lose your footing for a moment and half-recover
cards.contrast: Tripping is the cause; stumbling is the wobble that follows. You can also stumble over your words — the same idea applied to speech.
examples: She stumbled but caught the railing in time.
I stumbled over his name twice before I got it right.

cards.meaning: to walk unsteadily, as if about to fall over
cards.contrast: A stumble is one moment. Staggering goes on for several steps — from exhaustion, weight or a blow.
examples: He staggered in with four bags and dropped all of them.
She staggered back a step when the door swung open.

cards.meaning: to handle something clumsily, nearly dropping it
cards.contrast: Fumbling is with the hands; stumbling is with the feet. You fumble for keys in a dark bag, and you fumble a catch.
examples: I fumbled the phone and it landed face down.
He fumbled for the light switch for a good ten seconds.

cards.meaning: to shut or put down something with sudden force and noise
cards.contrast: Slamming is loud and forceful. Shutting is neutral. Banging is repeated noise, not one decisive movement.
examples: She slammed the door hard enough to shake the frame.
He slammed his laptop shut and walked out.

cards.meaning: to look at something very briefly
cards.contrast: A glance is a second or less. To GLARE is to look angrily. To STARE is to look for too long. To GLIMPSE is to barely catch sight of something.
examples: He glanced at his watch twice while I was talking.
I glanced at the message and put the phone away.

cards.commonError: Three syllables, not four. Not 'com-FORT-able' — the middle collapses: COMF-ta-ble.
Stress on the first syllable. Both SKED-yool and SHED-yool are standard; pick one and stay with it.
The 't' is usually silent: OF-en, not OF-ten.
The stress is on the very last syllable, and the first sounds like 'on', not 'en'.
Three syllables, not four. The second 'e' disappears entirely.
The last syllable is 'min', not 'mine'. Stress the middle.

cards.line: I looked at the numbers again this morning, and the problem isn't the budget. It's the timeline.
cards.marked: I looked at the numbers again this morning, / and the problem isn't the budget. // It's the timeline.

cards.line: We're not going to make the fifteenth. I want to tell you now rather than on the day.
cards.marked: We're not going to make the fifteenth. // I want to tell you now / rather than on the day.

cards.line: He asked whether the accounts had been checked, approved and closed.
cards.marked: He asked whether the accounts / had been checked, / approved / and closed.

cards.line: When the meeting finally started, forty minutes late, half the people who needed to be there had already left for lunch.
cards.marked: When the meeting finally started, / forty minutes late, // half the people who needed to be there / had already left for lunch.

cards.line: Revenue moved from four point two to five point one, which is about a twenty per cent jump.
cards.marked: Revenue moved / from four point two / to five point one, // which is about a twenty per cent jump.

cards.line: So there I was, standing outside the office at seven in the morning, with no keys and no phone.
cards.marked: So there I was, / standing outside the office at seven in the morning, // with no keys / and no phone.
